pr_title: X509 app: major cleanup of user guidance, documentation, and code structure
pr_body:
While adding tests to #13658 I came across various shortcomings in the user guidance of the `x509` app.
Like with several other apps, there are meanwhile a lot of options and their presentation to users has become a mess.
This is likely due to various incremental additions of options having grown wild without intermediate cleanup.

I spent quite some effort getting the presentation of the options in the help output and the documentation into a logical order
and fixing descriptions where they were outdated or unclear.
During this process I inevitably found a couple of minor bugs and fixed them, 
in particular regarding unexpected combinations of options and memory leaks of the `-clrext` option.

~I've also renamed the new `-force_pubkey` option to the more consistent and less 'aggressive' name `-set_pubkey`~
and did some minor improvements to the related tests.

~I've renamed the `-signkey` option to `-key` for consistency with the `req` app
and because this better reflects that usually also the public portion is used,
retaining the old `-signkey` option for backward compatibility.~

Moreover, this adds the `-copy_extensions` option, used when transforming x509 <-> req.
Fixes #3638
Fixes #6481
Fixes #10458
Partly fixes #13708
Supersedes #9449

##### Checklist
<!-- Remove items that do not apply. For completed items, change [ ] to [x]. -->
- [x] documentation is added or updated
- [x] tests are added or updated

@t8m, your recent change requests are fulfilled.

I've added a further related commit regarding `apps/x509.c`: 
Make `-x509toreq` respect `-clrext`, `-sigopt`, -and `-extfile` options
and prevent copying SKID and AKID extensions to CSRs, which make no sense there.

BTW, it's a historical accident that SKIDs and AKIDs are encoded as X.509 extensions rather than as genuine cert attributes.

> BTW, it's a historical accident that SKIDs and AKIDs are encoded as X.509 extensions rather than as genuine cert attributes.

ITU didn't define it, the IETF did.  i don't think anyone would say X509 is "minimal" but it really just has only what is strictly needed ... :)

I've further improved my most recent commit such that now the `-ext` option can be used to select which extensions to copy.
On this occasion I further simplified the overall structure of the code, removing major redundancies.

BTW, my two most recent commits also address memory leaks of the `-clrext` option, 
which surfaced in tests after I had used the same `X509_delete_ext(x, i)` pattern for `-ext`.

So I fixed both usages and added a warning to the doc of `X509v3_delete_ext()` and friends 
that their behavior (namely, not to deallocate their subject) is a bit counter-intuitive.
And yeah, we need a rebase to fix conflicts.

> And yeah, we need a rebase to fix conflicts.

Thanks @t8m for your further round of comments; 
I've addressed them and also fixed the recent merge conflicts.

Done.

> This one was very hard to review so for the next time I'd suggest avoiding sideline improvements if possible. Submit them as separate PRs to keep the main topic PR more manageable.

Yeah, unfortunately this PR became very bulky.

It started out by improving a few options of `x509` and their documentation,
but doing so I came across more and more issues related to these changes,
and I was forced to do some further fixes also in the crypto lib to get the tests through etc.

A couple of fixes could have been done independently, though,
and I actually took a few of them to a separate PR, such as #13714.
The later addition of the `-copy_extensions` option would better have been done in a follow-up PR after this one would have been merged, but adding the same option to the `req` app I did not resist the temptation to add it here at the same time.

On the bright side, handling this all in one PR saved us from handling some 10+ separate PRs :wink:

If I had known in advance how much technical debt this PR would uncover and need to deal with I'd likely not have done it because it was a huge effort, which I ended up having to do in my spare time.

I appreciate your endurance also as a reviewer.

> Anyway this is really a good improvement of the code 

Pleased to hear!

>and it hopefully should not cause any serious regression.

I hope so, too.
(And if there is one, this would imply that there was a serious omission in the existing tests).

issue_context.title: The x509 and req apps should copy X.509 extensions when converting formats
issue_context.body:
When using the `X509` app to input and output certs (maybe just converting from PEM to DER) or 
when using the `req` app to input and output a CSR, 
any X.590 extensions in the input are copied.

In contract, when using the `x509` app with `-x509toreq` to convert a cert to a CSR or with `-req` for the opposite direction, or
when using the `req` app with `-x509` to convert a CSR to a cert (whereas the opposite direction is not supported),
any X.509 extensions in the input are not taken over. I find this at least counter-intuitive.
I'm currently cleaning up both apps in particular concerning their user guidance and will make clear that no extension are copied.
Yet I believe it would be better if X.509 extensions were copied also when converting between cert and CSR, at least optionally.

BTW, there is a huge overlap between these two apps, while on the other hand there are needless inconsistencies in their use. 
It would have been good, also in terms of code redundancy and maintenance, to have just one app that covers all their (pretty related) use cases.
comments:
Re the last thing you wrote, I find it clearer that there is a separate command to handle CSRs and a separate command to handle certs.

Regarding the matter of this issue, though, I couldn't agree more.  I vaguely recall that there was a time when automatic copying of extensions was frowned upon, especially for the `ca` command when making a cert (the argument there was that the authority should govern the extensions, not the certificate requestor), and it's possible that this impacted on how the `x509` and `req` commands.

>  vaguely recall that there was a time when automatic copying of extensions was frowned upon,

Normal CA's don't do this, of course. I think there was concern that someone would build a real CA around the OpenSSL app. Perhaps that isn't a concern any more. 👍 

But if you do change the behavior to copy over all extensions in the request, please do it by adding a new flag.  Don't quietly change the existing behavior.
It a recurring question : see also #6890, #10458 ( plenty more links here) or an old one #341.

>> BTW, there is a huge overlap between these two apps, while on the other hand there are needless inconsistencies in their use.
It would have been good, also in terms of code redundancy and maintenance, to have just one app that covers all their (pretty related) use cases.

> Re the last thing you wrote, I find it clearer that there is a separate command to handle CSRs and a separate command to handle certs.

Yeah, having just one command to handle both X.509 certs and X.509 cert requests may also be confusing.

For the remaining points in my above more general side remark I've just filed a separate issue: #13720.

> It a recurring question : see also #6890, #10458 ( plenty more links here) or an old one #341.

Oh my goodness, so many requests in that direction for that long time, and nobody has taken the time yet to fix the issue!
Now I see that the issue I've filed here is a generalization of #10458.

I'll fix it right away by adding a `-copy_extensions` option to both `x509` and `req`.

>  I vaguely recall that there was a time when automatic copying of extensions was frowned upon,

I mean, in some sense it still is, and @richsalz hit it on the head with "there was concern that someone would build a real CA around the OpenSSL app".  The first rule of being a CA is "know what you sign", and if you are blindly copying extensions that means you're not looking at them, and thus, don't know that you know what you're signing.

> The first rule of being a CA is "know what you sign"

Of course. Yet this issue is not about the CA (demo) app but about two rather low-level cert/CSR conversion tools.
There's a good thing about this bug: it made me study the `openssl` tool in detail. Couldn't believe this was a bug!
Finally, I've found the time to fix this also for the  `x509` app, as part of #13711.
